lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5, what is a glossary? (A list of special words and their meanings, in alphabetical order, at the end.) Today: write to inform, with a clear plan, precise words and helpful features.

An informative text explains a topic to someone who does not know it. Start with a title and an introduction that says what the reader will learn: "Volcanoes are openings in the Earth's crust. This text explains how they form."

Organise your ideas into sections, each with a heading (a subheading) that tells the reader what it is about: How volcanoes form, Why they erupt, Living near a volcano. Put the sections in a sensible order.

Develop each section with facts, definitions, examples and quotations. A definition explains a special word: "Magma is melted rock under the ground." An example makes it real: "Mount Etna, in Sicily, erupts often."
Use precise words, the subject's own terms: erupts, not goes off; molten, not really hot. Precise words teach the reader the subject's language and make your meaning exact.
Add features that help: a diagram with labels, a caption that says what a picture shows, bullet points for lists, and a glossary at the end.
Link ideas with words such as because, as a result, for example and in contrast, and keep a formal style. End with a conclusion that sums up the main points and why they matter.

Try it in the world: write a one-page guide to something you know well, such as building a raft in your world. Give it a title, two subheadings, a definition, a labelled drawing with a caption and a glossary. Next: write a narrative.

exercises.prompt: What does the introduction of an informative text do?
choices: says what the reader will learn
exercises.explain: The introduction names the topic and tells the reader what the text will explain.

exercises.prompt: Which feature is marked in orange?
exercises.hint: It is the line of words under the picture.
exercises.explain: A caption says what a picture or diagram shows.

exercises.prompt: A subheading tells the reader what one section is about.
exercises.hint: Look at the blue words on the page.
exercises.explain: True: subheadings help readers find the part they need.

exercises.prompt: Which word is the most precise? The volcano ___.
exercises.hint: Which word would a scientist use?
exercises.explain: "Erupted" is the exact word for a volcano throwing out lava, ash and gas.

exercises.prompt: Match each feature to its job.
exercises.hint: Think of where each one is on a page.
exercises.explain: Glossary: explains special words. Caption: says what a picture shows. Subheading: names a section. Introduction: opens the text.

choices: Lava is melted rock on the Earth's surface.
exercises.hint: A definition says what a word means.
exercises.explain: It explains what the word lava means.

exercises.prompt: Label the page: tap a word, then its number.
exercises.hint: The title is at the top; the subheading is in blue; the caption sits under the picture; the glossary is at the bottom.
exercises.explain: Title at the top, the blue subheading, the diagram with its caption under it, and the glossary at the bottom.

exercises.prompt: Put the parts of an informative text in order.
exercises.hint: What goes first, and what goes at the very end?
exercises.explain: Title, introduction, sections with subheadings, conclusion, then the glossary.

exercises.prompt: Which linking words fit? Magma is lighter than the rock around it. ___, it rises.
exercises.hint: Is the second sentence a result of the first?
exercises.explain: It rises because it is lighter: a result, so As a result fits.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences: formal or informal?
exercises.hint: Look for slang, short forms and exclamations.
exercises.explain: Formal: Volcanoes form where plates meet. Etna erupts often. Informal: Volcanoes are super scary! Lava's like, really hot.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best subheading for a section about what to do if a volcano erupts nearby?
exercises.hint: A subheading names exactly what the section covers.
exercises.explain: It tells the reader exactly what the section is about.

exercises.prompt: A glossary lists special words in alphabetical order with their meanings.
exercises.hint: Think of a small dictionary at the back.
exercises.explain: True: readers can look up any special word quickly.

exercises.prompt: Which conclusion is best for a text about volcanoes?
choices: Volcanoes are dangerous but build new land.
exercises.hint: A conclusion sums up the main points.
exercises.explain: It sums up both main ideas: the danger and the new land that volcanoes make.

choices: For example, Mount Etna has erupted many times.
Volcanoes are openings in the crust.
Magma rises because it is light.
exercises.hint: Which one names a real case?
exercises.explain: It gives a real volcano as a case of the idea.

exercises.prompt: What would help most to explain how a volcano erupts?
choices: a labelled diagram with a caption
exercises.hint: What shows how the parts work together?
exercises.explain: A labelled diagram shows the parts, such as the magma chamber and the crater, and how the magma rises.

exercises.hint: Start with the word being defined.
exercises.explain: "Magma is melted rock under the ground."

exercises.prompt: Which word is the most precise? Plants make food from sunlight. This is ___.
exercises.explain: Photosynthesis is the exact word for plants making food using light.

exercises.prompt: An informative text should include the writer's opinions about the topic.
exercises.explain: False: it informs with facts, definitions and examples; opinions belong in an argument.

exercises.prompt: Writing about volcanoes: sort each sentence. A definition, an example, or an explanation?
items: Magma is melted rock under the ground.
Mount Etna, in Sicily, erupts often.
Magma rises because it is lighter than rock.
A crater is the bowl at a volcano's top.
As a result, pressure builds until it erupts.
exercises.hint: A definition says what a word means; an example names a real case; an explanation says why or how.
exercises.explain: Definitions: magma and crater are explained. Examples: Etna and Vesuvius are real volcanoes. Explanations: because and as a result show why magma rises and why it erupts.
